content: A medication, also referred to as a medicine or drug, is any substance or combination of substances that is administered to humans or animals for the purpose of treating or preventing disease. Medications can also be used to assist in medical diagnoses. Commercially available medications are typically manufactured by pharmaceutical companies and are often protected by patents. Once the patent expires, other companies can produce equivalent versions of the drug, which are referred to as generic drugs. Medications can be classified in various ways, such as by their chemical properties, the method of administration, or the biological system they affect. One of the most comprehensive and widely used classification systems is the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) Classification System. Medications for the Gastrointestinal Tract or Digestive System Upper Digestive Tract: Medications include antacids, reflux suppressants, antiflatulents, antidopaminergics, proton pump inhibitors, H2-receptor antagonists, cytoprotectants, and prostaglandin analogues. Lower Digestive Tract: These include laxatives, antispasmodics, antidiarrhoeals, bile acid sequestrants, and opioids. Medications for the Cardiovascular System General Cardiovascular Medications: These include beta-receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, cardiac glycosides, antiarrhythmics, nitrates, antianginals, vasoconstrictors, vasodilators, and peripheral activators. Medications include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and alpha blockers. Coagulation Management: Includes anticoagulants, heparin, antiplatelet drugs, fibrinolytics, anti-hemophilic factors, and haemostatic drugs. Atherosclerosis and Cholesterol Management: Hypolipidaemic agents and statins are commonly used. Medications for the Central Nervous System These include hypnotics, anesthetics, antipsychotics, antidepressants (such as tricyclic antidepressants, monoamine oxidase inhibitors, lithium salts, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), anti-emetics, anticonvulsants, antiepileptics, anxiolytics, barbiturates, movement disorder drugs, stimulants (e.g., amphetamines), benzodiazepines, cyclopyrrolones, dopamine antagonists, antihistamines, cholinergics, anticholinergics, emetics, cannabinoids, and 5-HT antagonists. Medications for Pain and Consciousness The primary classes of analgesics include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, and other agents such as paracetamol, tricyclic antidepressants, and anticonvulsants. Medications for Musculoskeletal Disorders These include NSAIDs (including COX-2 selective inhibitors), muscle relaxants, neuromuscular drugs, and anticholinesterases. Medications for the Eye General Use: Adrenergic neuron blockers, astringents, and ocular lubricants. Diagnostic Use: Topical anesthetics, sympathomimetics, parasympatholytics, mydriatics, and cycloplegics. Anti-Bacterial Agents: Includes antibiotics, topical antibiotics, sulfa drugs, aminoglycosides, and fluoroquinolones. Anti-Viral and Anti-Fungal Agents: Includes imidazoles and polyenes. Anti-Inflammatory Agents: NSAIDs and corticosteroids. Anti-Allergy Agents: Mast cell inhibitors. Anti-Glaucoma Agents: Adrenergic agonists, beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, hyperosmotics, cholinergics, miotics, parasympathomimetics, prostaglandin agonists, and prostaglandin inhibitors. Medications for the Ear, Nose, and Oropharynx These include sympathomimetics, antihistamines, anticholinergics, NSAIDs, steroids, antiseptics, local anesthetics, antifungals, and cerumenolytics. Medications for the Respiratory System These include bronchodilators, NSAIDs, anti-allergic agents, antitussives, mucolytics, decongestants, corticosteroids, beta-receptor antagonists, anticholinergics, and steroids. Medications for Endocrine Disorders These include androgens, antiandrogens, gonadotropins, corticosteroids, growth hormones, insulin, antidiabetic agents (e.g., sulfonylureas, biguanides like metformin, thiazolidinediones), thyroid hormones, antithyroid drugs, calcitonin, diphosphonates, and vasopressin analogues. Medications for the Reproductive and Urinary Systems These include antifungals, alkalizing agents, quinolones, antibiotics, cholinergics, anticholinergics, anticholinesterases, antispasmodics, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, selective alpha-1 blockers, and sildenafil. Contraceptive Medications These include hormonal contraceptives, ormeloxifene, and spermicides. Medications for Obstetrics and Gynecology These include NSAIDs, anticholinergics, haemostatic drugs, antifibrinolytics, hormone replacement therapy, bone regulators, beta-receptor agonists, follicle-stimulating hormones, luteinizing hormones, LHRH, gamolenic acid, gonadotropin release inhibitors, progestogens, dopamine agonists, estrogens, prostaglandins, gonadorelin, clomiphene, tamoxifen, and diethylstilbestrol. Medications for Skin Conditions These include emollients, anti-pruritics, antifungals, disinfectants, scabicides, pediculicides, tar products, vitamin A derivatives, vitamin D analogues, keratolytics, abrasives, systemic antibiotics, topical antibiotics, hormones, desloughing agents, exudate absorbents, fibrinolytics, proteolytics, sunscreens, antiperspirants, and corticosteroids. Medications for Infections and Infestations These include antibiotics, antifungals, antileprotic drugs, antituberculous drugs, antimalarials, anthelmintics, amoebicides, antivirals, and antiprotozoals. Medications for Immunology These include vaccines, immunoglobulins, immunosuppressants, interferons, and monoclonal antibodies. Medications for Allergic Disorders These include anti-allergic agents, antihistamines, and NSAIDs. Medications for Nutrition These include tonics, iron preparations, electrolytes, parenteral nutritional supplements, vitamins, anti-obesity drugs, anabolic drugs, haematopoietic drugs, and food product drugs. Medications for Neoplastic Disorders These include cytotoxic drugs, sex hormones, aromatase inhibitors, somatostatin inhibitors, recombinant interleukins, granulocyte colony-stimulating factors (G-CSF), and erythropoietin. Medications for Diagnostic Purposes Contrast media are used for diagnostic imaging. Legal Considerations Medications are categorized as either over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, which can be purchased without a prescription, or prescription-only medicines (POM), which require authorization from a licensed medical practitioner. The distinction between OTC and prescription drugs varies by jurisdiction. The International Narcotics Control Board of the United Nations enforces global regulations prohibiting certain medications, maintaining a list of restricted substances. OTC drugs are considered safe for general use when taken as directed. Some countries, such as the United Kingdom, have an additional category of pharmacy-only medicines, which can only be sold under the supervision of a pharmacist. Naming of Drugs It is often preferable to refer to medications by their generic names rather than their brand names to avoid confusion. Related Topics Polypharmacy: The concurrent use of multiple medications (five or more), which can increase the risk of adverse effects. Zoopharmacognosy: The study of how animals use natural substances, including non-food items, for medicinal purposes.
